name: Creole Cottage

revival_periods.note: Revived in New Orleans through the Vieux Carré Commission (established 1936) and the restoration work of Richard Koch and Samuel Wilson Jr., more as preservation practice than as new suburban production.

regions: New Orleans (Vieux Carré, Faubourg Marigny, Tremé)
Bayou Teche and the Acadian parishes
geography.hearth: New Orleans and the river parishes above it, on French plan habits reworked through a century of Caribbean practice

lineage.note: The steep double-pitched roof on Norman trusses and the colombage wall are the direct structural inheritance; everything about the plan's climatic behaviour is a New World development.

description.short: A one-storey four-room house with no hallway, two or four equal front doors, and a roof that either extends over a shallow gallery or projects as a bracketed abat-vent, built at the front lot line from the Gulf Coast to the bayous.
description.long:
The Creole cottage is the densest piece of climatic reasoning in American vernacular building, and its most radical decision is a negative one: there is no hall, and there is no front door. There are two front doors, or four, and they are the same size and the same importance, one per front room. Circulation happens by walking from room to room through paired French casement doors, or by stepping outside onto the gallery and re-entering somewhere else. In a climate where a corridor is a dead space with a single opening and no breeze path, this is not primitivism. It is the correct answer, arrived at by people who had been living in the Caribbean for a century before they got to Louisiana.

The plan is a square of four rooms, two wide and two deep, roughly thirty-six by thirty-six feet, with the two front rooms formal and the two rear rooms private. Behind them, at the back wall, two small enclosed rooms — the cabinets — project at the corners with an open recessed loggia between them; one cabinet usually contains the stair to the garret. Chimneys are internal, on the party wall between the paired rooms, so the masonry heats two rooms and stays inside the envelope. Ceilings run eleven to thirteen feet, which puts the hot air well above anyone's head and lets the full-height doors work as a chimney for the room.

The front is where the type divides. The rural and early urban cottage carries a posted gallery six to ten feet deep, roof continuous over it at a flattened pitch. The dense urban cottage, built to the front lot line on Bourbon or Dauphine or Royal, cannot have posts on the banquette, so it uses the abat-vent: the roof plane, or a separate shed, projecting thirty to forty-eight inches over the sidewalk on wrought-iron rods or timber brackets, with nothing touching the ground. That detail is unique to the Gulf Creole tradition and is the single fastest way to identify the type from a passing car.

Walls are colombage — heavy cypress posts with soft brick nogging (briquette-entre-poteaux) or mud-and-moss bousillage — stuccoed on masonry-fronted work and weatherboarded elsewhere, because the local brick was too soft to be left in the weather. The roof is steep, forty to fifty degrees, hipped or side-gabled, and where a gallery exists the pitch breaks at the wall plane.

Inside, on a July afternoon with the blinds closed and the doors open, it is a genuinely comfortable building without a machine in it: high ceilings, deep shade, cross-draught through every room, twelve-inch cypress floorboards two feet off the ground, and light coming in low and green off the shutters. The type persisted into the 1860s almost unchanged for the good reason that nothing better was available.

defining_characteristics: Four-room square plan, two rooms wide and two deep, with no interior corridor and no principal front door
Two (or four) equal full-height French casement doors on the front elevation, one serving each front room
Rear loggia recessed between two projecting corner cabinets, one usually containing the stair
Either a posted galerie 6–10 ft deep with a pitch break at the wall plane, or an abat-vent projecting 30–48 in on iron rods or brackets with no posts
Steep side-gable or hipped roof at 40–50 degrees over the body of the house
Colombage frame with briquette-entre-poteaux or bousillage infill, stuccoed or weatherboarded
Internal chimneys on the partition between paired rooms; ceilings 11–13 ft; floor raised 12–36 in on low brick piers
diagnostic_tells: Two front doors of identical size with no window between them, and no way to tell which is 'the' entrance
An abat-vent — a roof overhang with brackets or rods and no posts — over the sidewalk
Rear elevation showing a recessed open bay with a small square room at each end
Exterior louvred blinds on doors rather than on windows, because the openings are doors
Floor plate visible above grade on low brick piers, with no basement and no water table

distinguished_from.difference: Both are one-storey New Orleans types with no corridor, but the shotgun is one room wide with the gable to the street and rooms in single file; the Creole cottage is two rooms wide and two deep with the eave to the street. The shotgun is also later — post-1810 — and Afro-Caribbean in its transmission.

Same plan logic, radically different section. The raised house sits its principal floor eight to twelve feet up on a full masonry service storey and is reached by an exterior stair to the galerie; the cottage sits at or near grade on low piers.

After about 1830 many Creole cottages acquire Greek Revival door surrounds, wider frieze boards and square box columns. The plan test is decisive: a Greek Revival cottage has a central hall and one front door; a Creole cottage has neither.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Four equal cells sized by cross-ventilation and by the cypress beam, with the gallery or abat-vent depth set by the summer sun angle at the latitude of New Orleans.
typical_ratios: Overall body 32–40 ft wide × 30–38 ft deep; each room 15–19 ft square
Ceiling 11–13 ft on the principal floor
Roof 40–50 degrees on the body; gallery slope 20–30 degrees
Galerie depth 6–10 ft; abat-vent projection 30–48 in
French door opening 5 ft 6 in – 6 ft 6 in wide overall × 8–10 ft high
Floor 12–36 in above grade on brick piers
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Four bays: door–window–window–door, or door–door–door–door. Even-numbered and centreless by design; there is no privileged bay.

massing_affinities.note: The rural version with a posted galerie across the front.
Where flooding forces the whole cottage up onto a low masonry storey.
Superficially similar in room count only; the entry logic is entirely different.

constraints.statement: No interior corridor. Each of the two front rooms has its own exterior door on the front elevation, and every habitable room has openings on two walls.

Ceiling height not less than 11 ft on the principal floor; openings are full-height French casement doors reaching to within 12–18 in of the ceiling. An 8 ft ceiling defeats the stack ventilation the whole type depends on.

test.note: 11ft converted to inches exactly (132in) to match the vocabulary variable's unit.

constraints.statement: Front shelter is either a posted galerie not less than 6 ft deep with a roof pitch break at the wall plane, or an abat-vent projecting 30–48 in on brackets or rods with no posts to grade. A 4 ft posted stoop is neither and belongs to no phase of the type.
Finished floor 12–36 in above grade on brick piers; chimneys internal on the partition between paired rooms, never on the exterior gable wall.

test.note: The chimney-position clause in the same statement is categorical and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Exterior louvred blinds on every opening, leaf width equal to half the clear opening so that a closed pair exactly covers it, hung on strap hinges with holdbacks.

exemplars.name: Lafitte's Blacksmith Shop
exemplars.note: Briquette-entre-poteaux with a steep hipped roof; among the oldest surviving structures in New Orleans and the clearest surviving statement of the urban cottage before the Spanish-period fires.
exemplars.why: The node's own note calls it 'the clearest surviving statement of the urban cottage before the Spanish-period fires', and HABS LA-24 recorded it as 'an example of the small cottage type in New Orleans of over a century ago, and is one of the very few remaining'.

exemplars.name: Fontenette-Bienvenu House
exemplars.location: 201 North Main Street, St. Martinville, Louisiana
exemplars.note: A one-and-a-half-storey Creole cottage of colombage construction with Federal detailing — the type absorbing Anglo trim while keeping its plan. Listed on the National Register 1997, delisted 2024.
exemplars.why: The Bayou Teche expression: a colombage cottage of 1817 with Federal detailing (the node's own note, echoed by the register-derived description), on the Teche rather than in the Vieux Carre, and now delisted, which is a fact about the register and not about the house.

exemplars.name: Kent Plantation House
exemplars.note: Bousillage Creole house, the oldest standing structure in Rapides Parish; a raised cottage version of the same four-room, no-corridor plan with its outbuildings intact.
exemplars.why: The Red River reach of the type: the node's own note calls it the oldest standing structure in Rapides Parish and a raised-cottage version of the four-room, no-corridor plan, and the loc.gov record for HABS LA-1303 calls it the oldest known standing structure in central Louisiana.

exemplars.name: La Rionda Cottage
exemplars.note: A Vieux Carre cottage of 1811 by Antonio La Rionda, and the plan paragraph of this node measured: four rooms in a square, 29 by 40-9, two front doors and two front windows straight on the banquette, two chimneys on the spine wall each serving a pair of rooms, an open loggia behind between a cabinet and a kitchen, and a gable roof carried out over the sidewalk. Restored by the city under Richard Koch in 1940 and drawn by HABS.
exemplars.why: HABS LA-192 states the whole plan in one sentence -- 29'-0" x 40'-9", 'four rooms arranged in a square', an open loggia between a cabinet and a kitchen, two chimneys on the central wall, a gable roof with a sidewalk overhang -- which is the node's plan paragraph measured.

exemplars.name: Maison Olivier
exemplars.note: The Teche country's raised Creole cottage of about 1815, listed on the register as the 'Acadian House' and a National Historic Landmark since 1974: brick below, colombage above, a gallery across the front and the four-room, no-corridor plan behind it. Kept by the Longfellow-Evangeline State Historic Site, the first state park in Louisiana, which is why it is the Bayou Teche house a reader is shown.
exemplars.why: The register lists it (as 'Acadian House', NHL 1974) and HABS LA-1276 recorded it as 'Olivier House'; the Longfellow-Evangeline site keeps it as the Teche's raised Creole cottage of about 1815, the node's Bayou Teche region made specific in one well-documented building.

exemplars.name: LaPointe-Krebs House
exemplars.note: The Gulf Coast's oldest house and Mississippi's only French-period building above ground: a cypress-and-cedar frame filled with oyster-shell concrete, a bousillage room added to the west, two stuccoed brick stacks, a broken-pitch gable roof over porches on three sides, and dates offered from 1721 to 1772. The Creole plan in its coastal materials, sixty miles east of the parishes.
exemplars.why: SAH Archipedia calls it 'the oldest building in Mississippi, the sole above-ground structure remaining from Mississippi's French period', and HABS MS-18 recorded its oyster-shell-concrete frame walls and three-sided porch -- the Mississippi Gulf Coast reach the node's geography names.

exemplars.name: Badin-Roque House
exemplars.note: The Cane River's rarest survivor: a one-storey cottage of cedar posts set in the ground and filled with bousillage, 27 by 30 feet under an unbroken steep roof cantilevered over the front gallery, on Isle Brevelle in the Creole community of the Metoyers. One of four poteaux-en-terre houses known to stand in the country, dated anywhere from the 1770s to the 1830s depending on who is asked, and drawn by HABS.
exemplars.why: HABS LA-1361, the Cane River area survey, measures it at 27' x 30' and records it as a poteaux-en-terre house of which 'only three other French Creole examples are known', the Natchitoches reach of the node's geography in its rarest constructional form.

sources: Jay D. Edwards, 'The Origins of Creole Architecture', Winterthur Portfolio 29 (1994)
Jay D. Edwards and Nicolas Kariouk Pecquet du Bellay de Verton, A Creole Lexicon: Architecture, Landscape, People (2004)
Jessie Poesch and Barbara SoRelle Bacot, eds., Louisiana Buildings, 1720–1940 (1997)
Dell Upton and John Michael Vlach, eds., Common Places: Readings in American Vernacular Architecture (1986)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: creole-cottage-vernacular is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The four-room square plan — no corridor, every room cross-ventilated, size set by breeze reach rather than ratio — is exactly this pack's own subject; its 'THE SQUARE CELL' rule (module by module, a base unit added and extended rather than proportioned, after Glassie's structural analysis of Virginia folk housing) describes this cottage's own room-by-room additive logic closely, even though Glassie's own fieldwork was Virginia rather than Louisiana.

As with the parent style: French casement doors 5'6"-6'6" wide sit within opening-proportion's wide-leaf band where its 2:1 ratio is native rather than forced, and the pack's door-from-storey rule (storey/3.5) is a reasonable proportional starting point for an 11-13 ft ceiling. Preferred over sash-light for the same reason as the parent style: these are doors, not sash windows, and sash-light's glass-supply arithmetic has nothing to derive from here.

The node that shows both of the pack's lighter regimes side by side in one sentence: 'either a posted galerie 6-10 ft deep with a pitch break at the wall plane, or an abat-vent projecting 30-48 in on iron rods or brackets with no posts.' Those are two of the pack's three depth rules stated as alternatives on one building type, which is the clearest evidence in the corpus that depth follows carrying strategy rather than taste. The abat-vent band it gives is the same one `styles/regency.json` gives for its cast-iron balconette, independently.

Colombage with 'briquette-entre-poteaux or bousillage infill, stuccoed or weatherboarded' -- the same system in a fourth language, and the node that makes the pack's climate conflict concrete. The infill here is named for what fills it (little bricks between posts; mud-and-moss) and the wall is then COVERED, which is the historical norm the pack argues for and which revival work reverses. `balcony-gallery` and `room-vernacular` hold this node's other systems and neither touches the wall.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes place it on the peripteral temple, the Roman arch order and the colossal portico -- how many columns there are, where they stand and what they stand on -- and the three rules it actually delivers to this node are a portico taking half to three fifths of the front, a centre bay opening a third wider 'to frame the entrance', and a stair up one face of a podium. The node's front is four bays, even-numbered, with no privileged bay, and its own tell says there is 'no way to tell which is the entrance': there is no centre for the centre-bay rule to widen and no plain wall each side for a portico to be an event against. Its front shelter is stated as an exclusive either/or -- a posted galerie not less than 6 ft deep, or an abat-vent projecting 30-48 in on brackets or rods with no posts to grade -- and neither is the two- or three-rank column porch the pack's porch_type delivers, while its floor sits 12-36 in above grade on brick piers rather than on a crepidoma or a podium. The pack names the difference from the other side itself, calling the Southern plantation's wrapped colonnade 'a Creole gallery with a Greek order on it'.
declined_packs.quote: Even-numbered and centreless by design; there is no privileged bay
declined_packs.note: Governs 3 slots and declining strands all three: composition_parti, porch_type and steps_and_stoop each lose all dimensioning, with no pack behind them. Accepted as honest -- the node states its own galerie depth (6-10 ft), abat-vent projection (30-48 in) and floor height above grade (12-36 in), and no dimension beats a podium-and-portico dimension on a house that admits neither.
